Sold
sōld
v. (past of sell; in Scripture the word for a brother betrayed, a birthright squandered, and a man under sin)
Past tense of sell, Anglo-Saxon sellan, which originally meant simply to give or hand over — the commercial sense came later. The older meaning survives in the Bible's uses, where what is sold is very often handed over rather than traded.

Biblical Definition

Sold marks the Bible's worst bargains and its best. The worst are three. Esau “sold his birthright unto Jacob” (Gen 25:33) for a meal, and Hebrews calls him a profane person for it. Joseph's brothers “sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver” (Gen 37:28) — and Joseph himself later names the providence over it without excusing the crime: ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good. And Paul describes the natural condition of every man under the law: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom 7:14) — not a customer of sin but a slave sold into it, which is why the remedy has to be redemption and not reform. Against these stands the best bargain in Scripture, made by a merchant who knew what he had found: “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Mat 13:46) — a man who liquidates everything and counts it no loss.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives sold as the past tense and participle of sell, and defines sell as to transfer property to another for an equivalent in money — noting the Scripture use of being sold under sin.

expand to see more

SOLD, pret. and pp. of sell.

SELL, v.t. To transfer property, or the exclusive right of possession, to another for an equivalent in money.

2. To betray; to deliver or surrender for money or reward; as, to sell one's country.

3. In Scripture, to give up to the power of another; as, the Lord sold them into the hand of Jabin. Judges iv.

Note. Sold under sin, that is, wholly under its dominion, as a slave sold to a master.

Key Scripture

Gen 25:33 — "And Jacob said, Swear to me this day; and he sware unto him: and he sold his birthright unto Jacob."

Gen 37:28 — "Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt."

Rom 7:14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin."

Mat 13:46 — "Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it."

Modern Corruption

Rom 7:14 is used to normalise defeat — every Christian permanently “sold under sin” — and the pearl parable is inverted into a lesson about what the sinner must pay.

expand to see more

Romans 7 has been made into a charter for resignation, as though Paul were describing the settled and unimprovable condition of the believer. The chapter is describing a man under law and without power, and the argument does not stop there: chapter 8 opens with no condemnation and proceeds to the Spirit of life making free from the law of sin and death. Whichever way the interpretive question about Paul's reference is settled — and the Reformed tradition has held both readings — nobody may take “sold under sin” as the last word, because Paul does not. The believer is bought, not still on the block.

The pearl parable is regularly preached as a call to give up everything for Christ, which is true elsewhere in the Gospels but is not what this parable says. The merchant sells all he has because he has found something worth more than everything he had — the transaction is not a sacrifice but an obvious profit, and he goes away richer. Esau in Gen 25:33 is the exact photographic negative: a man who values a thing of infinite worth at the price of one meal because he wants the meal now. Both parables are about appraisal, and the question they put to the reader is what he thinks the kingdom is worth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon sellan, to hand over; rendering Hebrew makar (H4376), to sell, and Greek pipraskō (G4097) and poleo (G4453), to sell.

expand to see more

Anglo-Saxon sellan — to give, hand over; the commercial sense is a later narrowing.

Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; used both of commerce and of God delivering Israel into an enemy's hand (Jdg 2:14; 4:2).

Greek pipraskomai — perfect passive in Rom 7:14, pepramenos hupo ten hamartian, “having been sold under sin”: a completed transaction with a standing result.

Greek poleo (G4453) — to sell; the merchant of Mat 13:46 who sold all that he had.

Heb 12:16 — Esau, “who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright”, named a profane person for it.

Usage

"“He sold his birthright” — an infinite inheritance appraised at one meal."

"“Sold Joseph… for twenty pieces of silver” — the price of a boy, and a providence over a crime."

"“Sold all that he had, and bought it” — not a sacrifice but an obvious profit."
